Toward a Multidimensional CDI-CAT: Noun/Predicate Bias in Cantonese

George Kachergis

2026-09-17

Motivation

This replicates the pipeline built for Japanese (multidim/06-noun-predicate-cat-summary.Rmd) on Cantonese, as a cross-linguistic check of whether the same noun/predicate bifactor CAT design generalizes to a second, typologically different language. Unlike Japanese, this repo has no local Cantonese response data, so item metadata and administration data were pulled directly from Wordbank via wordbankr. Scripts are in multidim_cantonese/01 through 04; this document loads their saved output rather than refitting anything.

items <- read_csv(here("multidim_cantonese/item_lexical_categories.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
efa_loadings <- read_csv(here("multidim_cantonese/efa2_loadings.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
bifactor_items <- read_csv(here("multidim_cantonese/bifactor_item_params.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
bifactor_scores <- read_csv(here("multidim_cantonese/bifactor_scores.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
  mutate(noun_predicate_bias = S1_noun - S2_predicate)
cat_summary <- read_csv(here("multidim_cantonese/cat_simulation_summary.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
resp_data <- readRDS(here("multidim_cantonese/noun_predicate_response_data.Rds"))

# Japanese results, for the cross-linguistic comparison in Section 6
jp_items <- read_csv(here("multidim/item_lexical_categories.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
jp_bifactor_scores <- read_csv(here("multidim/bifactor_scores.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
jp_cat_summary <- read_csv(here("multidim/cat_simulation_summary.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
jp_resp_data <- readRDS(here("multidim/noun_predicate_response_data.Rds"))

1. Data source and item classification

Cantonese Wordbank has a single WS form (16-30 months, no WG), 804 word items. Unlike the Japanese pipeline (which used a locally-maintained item CSV), item metadata and response data come directly from wordbankr::get_item_data() / get_instrument_data(). Items are classified the same way as for Japanese: Wordbank’s own lexical_category field already collapses verbs+adjectives into a single “predicates” class for Cantonese too (confirmed by an exact crosstab match between our category-based mapping and Wordbank’s own coding), so action_words/descriptive_words were kept separate as lexical_class while also providing the 2-way pos2 (noun/predicate) collapse used for the CAT.

items %>%
  count(lexical_class, pos2) %>%
  arrange(pos2) %>%
  kable(col.names = c("Lexical class", "CAT dimension (pos2)", "N items"),
        caption = "Cantonese item counts by lexical class and CAT grouping.") %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)
Cantonese item counts by lexical class and CAT grouping.
Lexical class CAT dimension (pos2) N items
noun noun 316
function_word other 108
other other 124
adjective predicate 84
verb predicate 172

The content-word item bank is 572 items (316 noun, 256 predicate = 172 verb + 84 adjective) – larger than Japanese’s 478, both because Cantonese Wordbank has more items overall and because a larger share are content words.

2. Sample

Starting from 1208 Wordbank administrations, 2 non-producers and 1 child at ceiling were dropped, leaving 1205 administrations. Missingness in the content-word matrix was negligible (0.03%, vs. 12.6% for Japanese, since there’s no separate short-form data to reconcile here) and was imputed the same way (mirt::imputeMissing()) before the CAT simulation regardless.

3. Exploratory factor check

ggplot(efa_loadings, aes(x = F1, y = F2, color = pos2)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "F1 (general)", y = "F2 (noun vs. predicate)", color = "Item type",
       title = "Cantonese: exploratory 2-factor loadings") +
  theme_bw()

The same qualitative signature as Japanese: every item’s dominant loading is on F1 (mean 0.80 for nouns, 0.85 for predicates), with F2 a much smaller but reliably separating secondary factor (noun mean 0.082, predicate mean -0.042; Welch t = 11.6, p < .0001). One difference from Japanese: F1/F2 correlate r = .23 after oblimin rotation here, vs. r = -.015 for Japanese – less cleanly orthogonal, though F2 is still clearly a secondary, much smaller factor. This still supports a bifactor structure as the confirmatory model, which was fit next.

4. Confirmatory bifactor model

bifactor_items %>%
  mutate(own_specific = if_else(pos2 == "noun", S1_noun, S2_predicate)) %>%
  group_by(pos2) %>%
  summarise(mean_G = mean(G), mean_own_specific = mean(own_specific), n = n()) %>%
  kable(digits = 2, caption = "Mean general (G) and own-specific-factor loadings by item type.") %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)
Mean general (G) and own-specific-factor loadings by item type.
pos2 mean_G mean_own_specific n
noun 3.06 1.08 316
predicate 3.13 1.01 256 
rel <- empirical_rxx(bifactor_scores %>%
                        select(G, S1_noun, S2_predicate, SE_G, SE_S1_noun, SE_S2_predicate) %>%
                        as.matrix())
tibble(dimension = names(rel), empirical_rxx = rel) %>%
  kable(digits = 2, caption = "Empirical reliability of full-item-bank (non-adaptive) factor scores.") %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)
Empirical reliability of full-item-bank (non-adaptive) factor scores.
dimension empirical_rxx
G 0.98
S1_noun 0.86
S2_predicate 0.80

Reliability is notably higher than Japanese for the specific factors (S1 = .86, S2 = .80, vs. Japanese’s .71/.64) – consistent with the larger item bank and sample.

ggplot(bifactor_scores, aes(x = production, y = noun_predicate_bias)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.1) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE) +
  labs(x = "Total production (sum score)", y = "Noun/predicate bias (S1 - S2)",
       title = sprintf("r = %.2f", cor(bifactor_scores$production, bifactor_scores$noun_predicate_bias))) +
  theme_bw()

The bias score decouples from vocabulary size even more cleanly than in Japanese: r = -0.11 with production (Japanese: -.16) and r = -0.09 with age (Japanese: -.17). As with Japanese, the S1/S2 EAP score correlation is non-trivial (r = 0.72, actually higher than Japanese’s .48) despite the model constraining them to be latently orthogonal – the same known bifactor artifact, more pronounced here.

5. CAT simulation

5.1 Item selection criterion

As with Japanese, Drule (D-optimal across all 3 dimensions) was compared against Wrule with weights down-weighting G; Drule again matched or beat Wrule on a 100-person subsample, so Drule was used throughout.

5.2 A stopping-rule lesson

The first full-sample simulation used min_SEM = c(0.3, 0.5, 0.5) – the same target used for Japanese, chosen from that language’s full-bank SE ceiling. For Cantonese this badly under-shoots: because the full item bank supports much better specific-factor precision here (median full-bank SE ≈ 0.26-0.32, vs. Japanese’s ≈ 0.50-0.52), a target of 0.5 is satisfied very early – the CAT was stopping after a mean of only 56-85 items even with a 100-200 item ceiling available, and correlation with the full-bank bias estimate stayed disappointingly low (r ≈ .75-.82).

cat_summary %>%
  kable(digits = 3, caption = "Cantonese CAT simulation: item budget vs. recovered precision.") %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)
Cantonese CAT simulation: item budget vs. recovered precision.
criteria max_items mean_n_items mean_SE_G mean_SE_S1 mean_SE_S2 r_bias_vs_full r_G_vs_full n_items_never_used
Drule 50 37.343 0.213 0.522 0.568 0.755 0.981 291
Drule 100 55.967 0.204 0.505 0.550 0.797 0.983 177
Drule 200 84.980 0.201 0.498 0.543 0.817 0.984 66
Drule (min_items=150 forced) 200 192.490 0.139 0.387 0.446 0.968 0.996 NA

Forcing more items administered (min_items = 150, tightened min_SEM = c(0.3,0.3,0.3), still capped at 200) resolved this: mean items rose to 192, and r(CAT bias, full-bank bias) jumped to .97 – better than Japanese’s best result (.95 at 200 items). This is the most important methodological finding from the Cantonese replication: the empirically-grounded min_SEM target used for Japanese was too loose when applied to a different item bank/sample with a better achievable ceiling, and premature SE-based stopping silently produced worse recovery than a longer, fixed-ish administration would have. This is worth revisiting for the Japanese CAT too, rather than assuming its min_SEM = 0.5 choice was well-calibrated just because it seemed reasonable at the time.

6. Cross-linguistic comparison

tibble(
  language = c("Japanese", "Cantonese"),
  n_administrations = c(nrow(jp_resp_data$d_demo), nrow(resp_data$d_demo)),
  n_content_items = c(ncol(jp_resp_data$d_mat_content), ncol(resp_data$d_mat_content)),
  n_noun = c(sum(jp_items$pos2 == "noun"), sum(items$pos2 == "noun")),
  n_predicate = c(sum(jp_items$pos2 == "predicate"), sum(items$pos2 == "predicate")),
  full_bank_reliability_S1 = c(0.71, 0.86),
  full_bank_reliability_S2 = c(0.64, 0.80),
  bias_vs_production_r = c(
    round(cor(jp_bifactor_scores$production, jp_bifactor_scores$S1_noun - jp_bifactor_scores$S2_predicate), 2),
    round(cor(bifactor_scores$production, bifactor_scores$noun_predicate_bias), 2)
  ),
  best_cat_recovery_r = c(0.95, 0.97),
  items_for_best_recovery = c(131, 192)
) %>%
  kable(digits = 2, caption = "Japanese vs. Cantonese: key numbers side by side.") %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)
Japanese vs. Cantonese: key numbers side by side.
language n_administrations n_content_items n_noun n_predicate full_bank_reliability_S1 full_bank_reliability_S2 bias_vs_production_r best_cat_recovery_r items_for_best_recovery
Japanese 939 478 312 166 0.71 0.64 -0.16 0.95 131
Cantonese 1205 572 316 256 0.86 0.80 -0.11 0.97 192

The core design – bifactor model, Drule item selection – transfers cleanly across two typologically different languages. Cantonese, with a larger item bank and sample, supports a more reliable bias measure at the full-bank level, but realizing that advantage in a CAT required noticing and correcting an under-calibrated stopping rule, not just porting the Japanese settings over.

7. Summary and open questions

  • Item bank: 572 items (316 noun, 256 predicate), pulled and classified directly from Wordbank, with the classification cross-validated exactly against Wordbank’s own lexical_category coding.
  • Model: the same bifactor structure holds – EFA shows one dominant general factor plus a small, reliable noun/predicate-separating second factor, and the confirmatory bifactor model decouples the bias score from vocabulary size/age (better than Japanese: r ≈ -.09 to -.11).
  • CAT: Drule selection; the min_SEM stopping target must be recalibrated per item bank/sample rather than reused across languages – this was the main actionable finding from the replication.

Open questions:

  1. Should the Japanese CAT simulation (multidim/04-05) be rerun with a tighter min_SEM / higher min_items floor, given the same under-shooting risk likely applies there too?
  2. Cantonese’s 3-way verb/adjective split (172 vs. 84 items) is even more asymmetric than Japanese’s (103 vs. 63) – worth checking before attempting a 3-way model for either language.
  3. Given Cantonese has no WG (short) form, is a similar dual-form imputation approach available if a deployed CAT wants to accept both short- and long-form partial administrations, or should Cantonese deployment assume WS-only from the start?
